label: Philosophy
title: Amor Fati – Why Nietzsche Wanted to Love Everything That Happens
description: Amor fati – the love of fate. Nietzsche wrote it as a New Year's wish in 1882, while illness had already taken his career. In this calm video essay we look at what he actually meant, how Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius had said something similar almost two thousand years earlier, his famous thought experiment of living your life again and again, and the crucial difference between loving your fate and simply giving up.

sections.text:
On the first days of January 1882, a man in Genoa sat down to write his wishes for the new year.

He was thirty-seven. He had been a professor at twenty-four, and he had lost that position because of his health. Headaches, eye pain and nausea kept him in bed for days at a time. His books barely sold. Most people would have wished for one thing in that situation: that things had gone differently.

Friedrich Nietzsche wished for something else. He wished to love what had happened. He gave that wish two Latin words. Amor fati. The love of fate.

It sounds almost absurd. So what did he mean, and why has this small phrase outlived nearly everything else he wrote?

sections.heading: A New Year's Wish

quote.lead: The passage opens the fourth book of The Gay Science, under the heading For the New Year.
quote.text: I want to learn more and more to see what is necessary in things as beautiful; then I shall be one of those who make things beautiful. Amor fati: let that be my love from now on!
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science §276

sections.text:
Notice what Nietzsche does not say. He does not say that everything is good, or that suffering is secretly pleasant. He says he wants to learn to see it differently. It is a practice, not a fact.

And he immediately adds what he will give up. He no longer wants to wage war against what is ugly. He does not want to accuse, not even to accuse those who accuse. Looking away, he writes, shall be his only negation. Someday, he hopes, he will be only a Yes-sayer.

This is the core of amor fati. Not a feeling that arrives on its own, but a direction you choose to turn your attention, again and again.

sections.heading: Older Than Nietzsche

quote.lead: The idea itself is much older. Around the year 100, the former slave Epictetus taught his students a single sentence that contains almost all of it.
quote.text: Do not seek for things to happen as you wish, but wish them to happen as they do happen, and your life will flow well.
quote.author: Epictetus, Enchiridion 8

sections.text:
Epictetus knew what he was talking about. He had grown up enslaved and walked with a lame leg for most of his life. His teaching rested on one distinction: some things are up to us, and most things are not. Our judgments and choices are ours. The body, reputation and the events of the world are not.

If you demand that the world obey your wishes, you will be disappointed every single day. But if you learn to want what actually happens, the same world stops being your opponent.

Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor who studied Epictetus closely, used a vivid image for this. In the fourth book of his Meditations, he compares the mind to a fire. A small flame is smothered by what is thrown on it. A strong fire takes whatever falls into it, turns it into flame and light, and rises higher because of it.

sections.heading: Your Life, Again and Again
sections.text:
Nietzsche pushed this idea further than anyone before him. A few pages after his New Year's wish, near the end of the same book, he describes a strange thought experiment.

Imagine that one night a demon creeps into your loneliest loneliness and tells you that you will have to live this life again. And not just once, but countless times. Every pain and every joy, every thought and every sigh, in exactly the same order. Even this moment, and this very sentence.

Would you throw yourself down, Nietzsche asks, and curse the demon who said this? Or have you ever experienced a moment so great that you would answer: you are a god, and I have never heard anything more divine?

This is the real test of amor fati. Not whether you can tolerate your life once, but whether you could say yes to all of it, forever.

Six years later, in Ecce Homo, written in the autumn of 1888, Nietzsche called amor fati his formula for greatness in a human being. To want nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity. Not merely to bear what is necessary, and still less to hide it, but to love it.

He wrote those lines only a few months before his mental collapse in Turin in January 1889. He never wrote another book.

sections.heading: Acceptance Is Not Giving Up
sections.text:
There is an easy way to misunderstand all of this. Amor fati can sound like resignation. Like a shrug. Whatever happens, happens.

But neither Nietzsche nor the Stoics were passive people. Epictetus spent his life teaching. Marcus Aurelius ruled an empire through war and plague. Nietzsche kept writing through years of illness, book after book, often in fragments because his eyes could not take more.

The difference lies in where the acceptance points. Resignation looks forward and says: nothing I do matters. Amor fati looks at what has already happened and says: this is now part of my material. The past cannot be changed. But what you build from it is still open.

Resignation stops at the wall. Amor fati uses the wall as the next step.

sections.heading: Making Material of What Happens

quote.lead: Marcus Aurelius wrote a line in his private notebook that reads almost like a prayer of amor fati.
quote.text: Everything harmonizes with me, which is harmonious to thee, O Universe. Nothing for me is too early nor too late, which is in due time for thee.
quote.author: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IV.23

sections.text:
How can this become something you actually do, and not just a nice idea? Here is one quiet exercise.

Think of something in your life you once wished had gone differently. Not the hardest thing. Start small. A rejection, a detour, a plan that fell apart.

Then ask three questions. What did this make possible that would not have happened otherwise? What did it teach me that I could not have learned in any other way? And if it had not happened, who would I be without it?

You do not have to find a perfect answer. Sometimes the honest answer is: I do not know yet. That is fine. Amor fati is not a verdict on your past. It is a way of staying open to what it can still become.

And please be gentle with the heavier things. Not every loss needs to be loved today. Nietzsche himself called it something he wanted to learn, more and more.

sections.heading: Saying Yes
sections.text:
Most of us spend a surprising amount of energy arguing with what has already happened. Replaying it. Rewriting it. Wishing the story had gone another way. As if enough thinking could still reach back and change a single line.

Amor fati offers a different kind of freedom. Not the freedom to change the past, which nobody has, but the freedom to stop fighting it.

A sick man in Genoa, without a job and almost without readers, decided to love his fate. The books he wrote in those years are still read all over the world. Not in spite of what happened to him, but in part because of it.

Perhaps the question is not whether your life went the way you planned. Perhaps it is whether you can turn what happened into flame and light.

short.title: Nietzsche's strangest wish – love everything that happens
short.hook: Could you live your life again?
short.text:
In January 1882, a sick man in Genoa wrote down his wish for the new year. He had given up his job as a professor because of his health. His books barely sold.

He did not wish that things had gone differently. He wished to love what had happened. Amor fati. The love of fate.

Then he asked a radical question. Imagine you had to live your exact life again, every pain and every joy, countless times. Would you curse it? Or say yes?

This is not resignation. It is deciding that what happened becomes your material.

The man was Friedrich Nietzsche.
